data.title: Savanna-based Agroforestry
data.short_summary:
Increased carbon sequestration in above- and below-ground tree biomass and soil carbon due to integration of trees into grazing lands.

Units: all raster data (.tif) are in tCO2e/ha/yr. All tabular data (.csv) are summarised in tCO2e/yr.
data.description:
This layer shows the climate benefit, as increased sequestration, resulting from establishing trees into grazing lands with little to no tree cover. These estimates are based on a global land cover dataset quantifying biomass within pasture land (Chapman et al., 2020), a modified layer derived from expert elicitations to identify tree cover in agricultural lands (Hyppolite et al., 2024), and combined with regionally-specific carbon sequestration estimates for silvopasture systems (Cardinael et al., 2018). Relevant agroforestry practices for pasturelands include Silvopasture, Hedgerow, and Parkland (with grassland as the starting condition). 

Consistent with the naturebase accounting framework, areas of overlap between cropland and non-cropland pathway extents were resolved using a proportional allocation approach. Cropland pathway mitigation was weighted by the fraction of each 1 km² pixel classified as cropland, while non-cropland pathway mitigation was weighted by the inverse proportion. For a detailed description of this methodology, see Section I(c), Cropland Extent, in the NCS Accounting Rules Narrative.

Units: all raster data (.tif) are in tCO2e/ha/yr. All tabular data (.csv) are summarised in tCO2e/yr.

To calculate the per hectare mitigation potential (density) of the NCS implementation extent in tCO2e/ha/yr: 
1) Find the total mitigation value: this is provided in the spreadsheet as [pathway]_tco2e
2) Find the NCS hectare extent: This is provided in the spreadsheet as [pathway]_ha
3) Divide the mitigation value by the NCS hectare extent: tCO2e/ha/yr = [pathway]_tco2e / [pathway]_ha

To calculate the per hectare mitigation potential (density) for each administrative area* in tCO2e/ha/yr: 
1) Find the total mitigation value: this is provided in the spreadsheet as [pathway]_tco2e
2) Find the administrative extent: This is provided in the spreadsheet as 'admin_ha'
3) Divide the mitigation value by the administrative extent: tCO2e/ha/yr in each administrative area = [pathway]_tco2e / admin_ha

*This is useful for comparison between administrative areas

Please consult the download package under 'Download Now' for comprehensive metadata and a detailed description.

data.data_caveats: Although Chapman et al. (2020) is one of the best-available current “agroforestry” maps, it provides only a coarse estimate of where agroforestry is and is not (Terasaki Hart et al. 2023). Additional work is needed to map where agroforestry systems occur and where they could feasibly be expanded. Moreover, the flux data from Cardinael et al. (2018) are similarly coarse and there is substantial opportunity to refine those estimates to reflect the configurations of specific rather than general system types (Terasaki Hart et al. 2023). The unmasked maximum extent was used for the silvopasture extent, derived from Sprenkle-Hyppolite et al., 2024
data.approach_and_methods: To estimate the extent of potential for additional trees in grazing lands, we modified a recent study that used expert elicitation to identify how much tree cover is possible in grazing lands without negatively impacting yield (Hyppolite et al., 2024). That paper combined the percentage of pixel area covered by trees in 2015 (Sexton et al., 2013) and grazing extent (Chapman et al., 2020). They then subtracted from that the estimated maximum extent of tree cover percentage recommended by experts for 53 regional cropping and silvopastoral systems (Hyppolite et al., 2024). The remaining map shows the maximum additional tree cover percentage possible in grazing lands. We applied an additional conservative filter to assess areas that fall in locations that are determined to be suitable for forest cover (Fesenmyer et al., 2025). The remaining map shows the additional tree cover percentage possible. From there, we applied flux values from Cardinael et al. (2018), averaging across silvopasture, hedgerow and parkland estimates per IPCC Climate Zone, multiplying mitigation by the possible additional tree cover percentage. Because not all biome by continent combinations have flux values in the Cardinael et al. dataset, we filled missing values with an increasingly coarse search. This means that we preferentially select biome by continent values first (e.g., Tropical Dry in Africa), then biome (e.g., Tropical Dry), followed by general zone (e.g., Tropical). We assumed SOC accumulation rates continued until 2035 based on Ma et al. (2020).
data.additionality: We assumed that all additional expansion would be additional given that market forces on agricultural lands tend toward tree clearance.
data.next_steps: We are currently working on a substantial refinement to the flux data by reviewing over 25,000 publications to find field-derived estimates of carbon stocks in agroforestry systems. Our final database pulls information from more than 1000 papers and will ultimately be publicly available. We will use this information to determine the principal drivers of variation in carbon stocks in agroforestry systems, and use that information to help calculate more precise carbon stocks for specific systems. We also hope to use a more sophisticated map of where agroforestry could be expanded in future iterations.
